body_html:
Literal translation mistakes in Spanish are the ones that make a sentence technically understandable but clearly foreign. As a translator, I spend my days turning English meaning into natural Spanish, and the rule I follow is simple: translate the idea, not the words. Below are the literal translations I see most often from learners, grouped by type, with the natural Spanish you should use instead.

Key takeaways
  • Spanish often uses tener where English uses “to be”: tengo hambre, tengo 30 años.
  • Some verbs look like English but mean something else: realizar, aplicar, atender.
  • Idioms almost never translate word for word.
  • When in doubt, ask how a native speaker would say it in that situation.
{{toc}}

Literal translation mistakes in Spanish with “to be”

English uses “be” for many physical states that Spanish expresses with tener (to have):

EnglishLiteral (wrong)Natural Spanish
I’m hungryEstoy hambreTengo hambre
I’m thirsty / cold / hotEstoy sed / fríoTengo sed / frío / calor
I’m 30 years oldSoy 30 añosTengo 30 años
I’m scaredEstoy miedoTengo miedo
You’re rightEstás correcto (stiff)Tienes razón
I’m in a hurryEstoy en prisaTengo prisa

Careful with estoy caliente for “I’m hot”: it usually means aroused. More in {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}}.

Verbs that look English but aren’t

English meaningLiteral trapNatural Spanish
to realizerealizar (= to carry out)darse cuenta: Me di cuenta de que…
to apply (for a job)aplicarsolicitar, postularse (Latin America)
to attend (a meeting)atender (= to serve, look after)asistir a
to support (a team, a person)soportar (= to put up with)apoyar
to make sensehacer sentidotener sentido
to removeremover (= to stir, in Spain)quitar, eliminar

These are false friends; the full list is in {{link:spanish-false-friends|Spanish false friends}}. The Fundéu RAE regularly flags anglicisms like aplicar for “apply for”.

{{image:2}}

Everyday phrases that change shape

EnglishLiteral (wrong)Natural Spanish
What’s your name?¿Qué es tu nombre?¿Cómo te llamas?
How old are you?¿Cómo viejo eres?¿Cuántos años tienes?
I miss youTe pierdo (= I lose you)Te echo de menos / Te extraño
Have a good time!¡Ten un buen tiempo!¡Que lo pases bien!
Have a nice dayTen un buen díaQue tengas un buen día
It’s my turnEs mi vueltaMe toca
I’m looking forward to itEstoy mirando adelanteTengo muchas ganas
Take careToma cuidadoCuídate

Many of these appear in {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Idioms: translate the meaning

  • It’s raining cats and dogs → Llueve a cántaros.
  • It’s a piece of cake → Es pan comido.
  • To cost an arm and a leg → Costar un ojo de la cara.
  • To be in the clouds → Estar en las nubes (this one matches!)
  • To pull someone’s leg → Tomarle el pelo a alguien.
  • Break a leg! → ¡Mucha suerte! (never ¡Rómpete una pierna!)

Grammar that English pushes in the wrong direction

  • Subject pronouns: English needs “I”, Spanish usually doesn’t. Yo trabajo, yo vivo, yo tengo in every sentence sounds heavy; say Trabajo en Madrid y vivo con mi pareja.
  • Possessives with body parts: “I washed my hair” → Me lavé el pelo, not mi pelo.
  • Gerunds as nouns: “Swimming is healthy” → Nadar es sano, not Nadando es sano.
  • Passive voice: “It was decided” often becomes Se decidió, not Fue decidido.
  • Phrasal verbs: “give up” is rendirse or dejar, not dar arriba.

Prepositions are another huge source of literal errors: see {{link:spanish-preposition-mistakes|Spanish preposition mistakes}}.

How I avoid literal translation as a translator

My own process has three steps. First, I read the whole English sentence and ask what it means in that situation. Second, I imagine a native Spanish speaker in that same situation and ask what they would naturally say. Third, I read my Spanish aloud; if it sounds like something no one would say at a café, I rewrite it. You can do the same as a learner, and reading bilingual books side by side trains exactly this skill.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrect
Realicé que era tarde.Me di cuenta de que era tarde.
Eso no hace sentido.Eso no tiene sentido.
Apliqué para el trabajo.Solicité el trabajo.
Soy 25 años.Tengo 25 años.
Atendí la reunión.Asistí a la reunión.
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. I realized I had forgotten my keys. (Me di cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves.)
  2. It doesn’t make sense. (No tiene sentido.)
  3. We’re very cold. (Tenemos mucho frío.)
  4. I miss my family. (Echo de menos a mi familia. / Extraño a mi familia.)
  5. That exam was a piece of cake. (Ese examen fue pan comido.)

See all the mistake families in {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Literal translation mistakes come from a good instinct, using what you know, applied in the wrong place. Train yourself to translate meaning: ask what a native speaker would say in the same moment. Learn tener hambre, darse cuenta and tener sentido as whole phrases, and your Spanish will stop sounding translated.

faq.q: What are common literal translation mistakes in Spanish?
faq.a: Using estar or ser instead of tener for hunger, age and fear; realizar for realize; aplicar for apply for a job; hacer sentido for make sense; and translating idioms word for word.

faq.q: How do you say “I realized” in Spanish?
faq.a: Me di cuenta. Realizar means to carry out or make happen, not to realize.
No. The natural expression is tener sentido: Eso no tiene sentido (That doesn’t make sense).

options: Me di cuenta de que estaba equivocado.

questions.explain: The natural phrase is tener sentido.
Idioms translate by meaning: pan comido.
